title: Starting full and ending clean
subtitle: A pressure gate holds dispatch until the first batches can be good, every batch closes on its token budget, and a cleanup mode drains the tail when the GPUs go quiet

stats.label: average time to assemble a batch
batch fill at the median, the ninetieth and the ninety-ninth percentile
integers each GPU registers: batch size, tokens, input length, model

lede: A batching broker is judged on its steady state, and its steady state is the easy part. The beginning and the end of a workload are where batches get small, caches get rebuilt and GPUs sit idle, and both needed their own mechanism. At the start of a run, items trickle in. A broker that dispatches the first trickle produces tiny batches and poor graph reuse, and the engine spends its first minutes doing badly what it could do well a moment later. So nothing is dispatched until staged and lane tokens together reach a release threshold. Packing follows the contract each GPU registered with.
quote: Once open, the gate stays open for the life of the process; it is a start condition rather than a throttle.
evidence: Token-aware scheduling: a release gate that holds dispatch until staged and lane tokens reach a threshold, so the first batches of a run are full.
High-throughput batch inference: every batch in a two-GPU run closed on its token budget, at about 100% fill at the median and tail percentiles, assembled in 523 µs on average.
Lock-free shared-memory IPC: same-host batches through a ring on huge pages with a compare-and-exchange claim loop, offset-addressed batches and read-only mapping by the consumer.
Workload tail handling: a cleanup mode with activation threshold 0 and a minimum batch of 1 that drains staged shapes and short lanes when the GPUs go quiet.
author: Corey James
